chief_complaint: sudden sharp unilateral pelvic pain, normal pregnancy test
hpi_details: A 26-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden sharp unilateral pelvic pain, normal pregnancy test. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks her appendix might have suddenly ruptured or flared up because the sharp pain hit so violently on one side.
concerns: She is worried that she will need emergency surgery and miss her sister's destination wedding this coming weekend.
expectations: She hopes to get an urgent ultrasound to find out what is wrong and receive fast-acting pain relief.

investigation_events.title: Urgent pelvic Doppler ultrasound
investigation_events.availability_message: Urgent pelvic Doppler ultrasound is now available. Gynecology should be involved promptly if the clinical concern for torsion persists.

results.value: 5.1 cm right ovarian hemorrhagic cyst with retracting clot and moderate echogenic pelvic free fluid; preserved ovarian arterial and venous flow

clinical_knowledge.topic: Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Hemorrhagic Ovarian Cyst: Pelvic ultrasound, pain control, monitor vitals for hemoperitoneum, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden sharp unilateral pelvic pain, normal pregnancy test

Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Hemorrhagic Ovarian Cyst.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Ovarian torsion without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Sudden severe onset.
management_principles: Plan for Hemorrhagic Ovarian Cyst: Pelvic ultrasound, pain control, monitor vitals for hemoperitoneum
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with sudden sharp unilateral pelvic pain and a negative pregnancy test; further assessment is needed to establish the cause.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Hemorrhagic Ovarian Cyst.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute unilateral pelvic pain; urgently evaluate for ovarian torsion, hemorrhagic cyst, appendicitis, and other surgical causes.
reference_soap.plan: Assess vital signs and abdominal/pelvic findings, obtain urgent pelvic ultrasound, and involve gynecology promptly if torsion is suspected. Provide analgesia and monitor for bleeding or hemodynamic instability.

teaching.diagnosis: Acute unilateral pelvic pain: urgently evaluate for ovarian torsion and cyst complication
teaching.one_liner: Patient with sudden sharp unilateral pelvic pain, negative pregnancy test, consistent with a hemorrhagic ovarian cyst.

must_ask.say: Did the pain start suddenly, and how severe is it on a scale of 1 to 10?
Have you confirmed you are not pregnant?
Have you felt lightheaded, or noticed your heart racing?

must_ask.objective: Ask about prior ovarian cyst history
must_ask.say: Have you ever been diagnosed with an ovarian cyst before?
We need an urgent ultrasound to check the ovary; treatment depends on whether this is a cyst complication, torsion, or another cause.

history.answer: I came in because I suddenly developed a sharp pain on the lower right side of my belly a few hours ago, and it has been getting worse.
It started suddenly about four hours ago while I was sitting at my desk, and the pain has been steadily increasing since then.
The pain is in my lower right abdomen and pelvic area, and it has stayed right there without moving anywhere else.
No, the pain doesn't radiate to my back, shoulder, or down to my groin.
It feels sharp and constant, like a steady aching pain rather than cramps that come and go.
It started around a 4 out of 10, but over the last couple of hours it has risen to about a 7 out of 10.
Walking around or shifting positions makes it hurt more, whereas lying still on my side gives me slight relief.
I've occasionally had mild twinges on that side during my monthly cycle, but never anything this sharp or severe.
I felt a little nauseous when the pain got really bad, but I haven't thrown up at all.
My bowel movements have been regular with my usual stool this morning, and there has been no diarrhea or blood.
No, I haven't felt feverish, and I haven't had any chills or shivering.
No, my eyes and skin look normal, and my urine and stool colors haven't changed.
I have no pain or burning when I urinate, and I haven't noticed any blood or need to go more frequently.
I felt a bit lightheaded and dizzy when I stood up earlier, but I haven't passed out.
No, there has been no vaginal bleeding, spotting, or unusual discharge.
No, my chest feels fine, and I haven't had any chest pain or difficulty breathing.

history.answer: I had a light sandwich for lunch, nothing greasy or unusual, and I haven't had any alcohol today.
I took one acetaminophen tablet about two hours ago, but it didn't really take the edge off.
No, I have never had an irregular heartbeat, blood clots, or any blood vessel problems.
I took a home urine pregnancy test right before coming to the clinic, and it was completely negative.
About a year ago during a routine checkup, my doctor mentioned finding a small benign cyst on my right ovary, but said it didn't need treatment.
Yes, alongside the worsening belly pain, I have been feeling unusually wiped out and exhausted today.
The pain came on so suddenly and fiercely on that side that I honestly thought my appendix was bursting.
I am supposed to fly out for my sister's wedding in two days, and I am terrified this pain means I need an emergency operation.
I really need an ultrasound to see what is happening in there and some strong medication to take the pain away.
I don't have any chronic medical illnesses like high blood pressure or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries, and I've never had to stay overnight in a hospital.
I don't take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I don't have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink socially, usually just a glass of wine or beer once or twice a month.
I work as an office clerk and live in an apartment with my roommate.
There's no family history of ovarian cancer, endometriosis, or other major medical issues.
I am currently sexually active in a monogamous relationship with my partner.
My cycle is very regular at twenty-eight days, and the first day of my last menstrual period was exactly two weeks ago.
We use condoms consistently and my period is not late, so I really don't think I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and temperature 36.8°C.
Mild conjunctival pallor noted without scleral icterus.
Abdomen is flat with no distension, scars, or visible pulsations.
Normal active bowel sounds heard throughout all four quadrants with no bruits.
Moderate tenderness to light and deep palpation in the right lower quadrant and right suprapubic region without generalized rigidity.
Mild localized rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant with no generalized peritoneal signs.
Mild localized tenderness near McBurney's point, but psoas, obturator, and Rovsing's signs are all negative.
Negative Murphy's sign with no right upper quadrant tenderness or inspiratory arrest.
Marked tenderness in the right adnexa and mild cervical motion tenderness without active vaginal bleeding or discharge.
